title: Male function matters: extending the preconditions for pollinator–prey conflict. A commentary on ‘Fatal attraction: flowers lure pollinators as prey in the carnivorous Drosera hookeri (Droseraceae)’
content: Plant–pollinator interactions are generally mutualistic, but in order to survive in nutrient-poor soils, carnivorous plants must perform a delicate evolutionary balancing act: they require insects both as prey, from which they derive essential nutrition, and as pollinators for pollen transfer among flowers. It has been assumed that most carnivorous plant species resolve this ‘pollinator–prey conflict’ (PPC) by evolving long flowering stalks, distinct visual signals that differentiate traps from flowers, or deployment of chemical signals to ensure that potential pollinators are not captured as prey. However, in this issue of Annals of Botany, Gross et al. (2026) report the results of a 14-year study of the Australian sundew Drosera hookeri that reveals a striking exception to this pattern. Drosera hookeri does not catch a random assortment of insects; its traps are specifically filled with its most important pollinators.
